summary: Anushrut Gupta (PromptQL) contends that the pursuit of perfect "data readiness" for AI is a futile myth. Organizations spend enormous effort cleaning data, yet enterprise data remains messy—inconsistent naming, null values, old schemas, and siloed systems. Historical fixes—Snowflake/Databricks migration (2019), MDM, semantic layers (2023)—fail because business domains change quarterly. McKinsey estimates Fortune 500 companies lose $250M annually to poor data quality. Manual semantic layers fail because business definitions involve infinite edge cases; knowledge graphs can't encode contextual business meaning or accommodate billion-row tables. The core problem: AI lacks the business's tribal language—terms like GM, conversion, active customer carry domain-specific meanings. PromptQL proposes an agentic semantic layer behaving like a day-zero smart analyst that continuously learns through user correction. An LLM generates plans in a domain-specific DSL; a deterministic runtime executes them, decoupling planning from answer generation to prevent hallucination. No RAG is used—data never returns to the LLM. A prompt learning layer improves the semantic graph over time, creating company-specific business language (e.g., AcmeQL for Acme). The semantic layer is version-controlled with rollback capability. Demonstrations showed the system self-correcting (discovering actual status values), executing complex multi-source workflows (databases, Zendesk, Stripe), learning table meanings from badly named tables (morg, plug, zorp), correcting unit assumptions (cents vs dollars), and learning that financial quarters start in February. By day 30, the system figured out 47 business terms, mapped relationships across 6 systems, discovered 12 calculation variants, and achieved 100% accuracy on complex tasks. A Fortune 500 food chain company evaluated 100 vendors and found only PromptQL delivered 100% reliable AI; a high-growth fintech company saw similar results on their hardest questions. Users can edit intermediate reasoning steps, and the AI learns from corrections, reducing months of onboarding work to immediate deployment.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and the Data Readiness Myth
sections.summary: Anushrut Gupta introduces himself as leading applied research at PromptQL. He polls the audience about deploying AI systems on imperfect data, noting everyone spends enormous time making data ready for AI but this perfect data dream will never materialize.

sections.title: Enterprise Data Messiness and Failed Historical Fixes
sections.summary: Illustrates messy data with real examples—inconsistent table/column names, null values, unclear field types, incompatible systems. Traces failed fixes: 2019 standardization via Snowflake/Databricks (40% complete), MDM teams still implementing, 2023 semantic layers that break quarterly. McKinsey stat: $250M lost annually per Fortune 500 company due to poor data quality.

sections.title: Limitations of Semantic Layers and Knowledge Graphs
sections.summary: Audience discussion reveals semantic layers need constant manual pruning and maintenance. Customer acquisition cost example shows infinite edge cases can't be manually predefined. Knowledge graphs/Graph RAG can't capture contextual business meaning like 'deals at risk' or accommodate billion-row tables. Neither is the solution.

sections.title: The Real Problem: AI Lacks Tribal Business Knowledge
sections.summary: The real problem is AI doesn't speak the business's language—terms like GM, conversion, quarter, active customer have domain-specific meanings. Human analysts possess tribal/tacit knowledge enabling 100% reliable answers with explanations. AI lacks this trust-building knowledge, which is the missing piece.

sections.title: Solution: Agentic Semantic Layer via PromptQL
sections.summary: Proposes an agentic semantic layer that behaves like a day-zero smart analyst, learning through correction. PromptQL uses a foundational LLM to generate plans in a domain-specific DSL (data retrieval, compute aggregation, semantics). Plans execute in a deterministic runtime without LLM involvement in answer generation, avoiding hallucination. No RAG—data doesn't return to the LLM.

sections.title: Live Demonstration of PromptQL
sections.summary: Demo shows self-correction on 'top 5 customers by revenue' query (discovering actual statuses are paid/pending, not succeeded). Complex multi-step workflow demonstrates cross-source orchestration (databases, Zendesk, Stripe), sentiment analysis, and dynamic credit issuance. User can edit AI's intermediate steps via pencil icon; AI learns from corrections.

sections.title: Continuous Learning and Self-Improvement
sections.summary: Explains the prompt learning layer that improves the semantic graph over time, creating company-specific business language (e.g., AcmeQL). Demonstrates learning with badly named tables (morg, plug, zorp)—AI samples rows to infer table meanings, corrects cents-to-dollars, and learns financial quarters start in February. Version-controlled semantic layer builds enable rollback. By day 30, the system learned 47 business terms, mapped 6 systems, discovered 12 calculation variants, achieved 100% accuracy. Customer testimonials: Fortune 500 food chain evaluated 100 vendors, only PromptQL worked; high-growth fintech saw 100% accuracy on hardest questions.

demonstrations: "Who are my top 5 customers by revenue?" — system self-corrected by discovering actual status values ("paid"/"pending") differed from its initial assumption ("succeeded")

Complex multi-step workflow: find unique orgs by email domains, identify org with 3rd highest revenue, analyze latest 30 support tickets with comments from Zendesk, summarize tickets, extract sentiment, create 5 sentiment categories, and issue $1,000–$5,000 credits via Stripe based on sentiment
User editing AI intermediate steps via pencil icon to redirect the plan, with AI learning from the correction
AI issuing a $3,000 refund based on neutral sentiment extracted from support tickets
Badly named tables demo: AI identified that zorp=employees, plug=departments, morg=junction table by sampling rows, then corrected budget from cents to dollars yielding 2 employees instead of 5
Anti-money-laundering demo: AI learned that the company's financial quarter starts in February, not January, and applied this to subsequent queries
